Jordan’s Nationwide Strike Ends as Government and Unions Reach Agreement

AMMAN—A nationwide general strike that brought much of Jordan’s public and private sectors to a standstill over the past week ended on Monday, after the government and union representatives reached a deal addressing wage concerns and social security reforms.

The industrial action, which began last Tuesday, affected transportation, education, banking, and retail services in major cities including Amman, Irbid, and Zarqa. The Jordanian Chamber of Commerce estimated that daily economic losses reached around 12 million dinars ($17 million) during the strike, as ports operated at limited capacity and logistics chains experienced significant disruptions.

The walkout was coordinated by the National Union Federation of Jordan (NUFJ), which called for higher public sector wages and modifications to the recently introduced pension law. “This was a necessary step to ensure that workers’ voices are heard,” said NUFJ President Khaled Abu Taleb at a press conference on Monday. “We are satisfied with the government’s willingness to engage in dialogue and reach a fair compromise.”

Under the agreement, the government pledged to raise the minimum monthly wage for public sector employees by 8% starting July 1 and to revise contentious pension clauses in consultation with union representatives. The Ministry of Labor also committed to establishing a joint committee to review additional grievances within the next three months.

Prime Minister Hani Al-Majali praised the “spirit of cooperation” that led to the resolution. “We recognize the concerns expressed by workers and are committed to building a more sustainable and just economic environment,” he said in a statement released Monday evening.

Businesses began reopening Tuesday, with transportation services and schools resuming normal operations. Local retail chain Al-Madina Stores reported that customer footfall returned to pre-strike levels within hours of the announcement. The Jordan National Bank said its branches were all operating as usual, though it warned of potential backlogs in processing.

Analysts cautioned that while the agreement ends immediate disruptions, lingering concerns over inflation and employment could trigger further unrest. “Structural issues remain,” said Lina Haddad, senior economist at Levantine Research Group. “But this compromise marks a positive step toward social stability and economic recovery.”
